This study introduces a comprehensive deep learning framework for detecting hate speech in accented Malayalam speech, integrating advanced feature engineering, class balancing, and robustness evaluation. A diverse dataset was curated from Malayalam YouTube videos and movies to capture phonetic, dialectal, and prosodic variations. Distinct acoustic features-including Zero Crossing Rate (ZCR), Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC), Root Mean Square (RMS), and Mel Spectrogram-were extracted, producing 162 feature vectors per utterance. Data augmentation techniques, including noise injection, time stretching, and pitch shifting, were applied to enhance diversity. A customized 1D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was developed for binary classification of hate and non-hate speech. Building upon the initial study, this extended research introduces SMOTE-based class balancing, speaker-independent validation, and robustness testing using Gaussian noise to simulate real-world acoustic distortions. Multiple models, including CNN, Support Vector Machine(SVM), Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM, were evaluated under stratified, hold-out, and noise-perturbed conditions. The CNN achieved an accuracy of 95.3%, F1-score of 0.966, and AUC of 0.998 on the noisy hold-out set, demonstrating strong generalization and noise resilience. These results confirm that the integration of balanced learnSing, multi-level validation, and robustness evaluation significantly enhances the reliability of hate speech detection in accented and low-resource Malayalam speech, S establishing a transferable framework for multilingual content moderation. JSON: Name: accented_malayalam_hate_speech_cnn Title: A 1D convolutional deep learning framework with advanced acoustic feature engineering for hate speech detection in accented Malayalam speech Short Hypothesis: Applying advanced acoustic feature engineering combined with SMOTE-balanced training and a 1D CNN will produce a statistically significant increase in F1-score on speaker-independent accented Malayalam hate speech detection compared to SVM and Random Forest baselines. Related Work: Prior work in hate-speech detection has largely focused on text or on well-resourced languages; audio-based approaches have used CNNs or multimodal fusion but rarely target regional accents. Classical methods (SVM, Random Forest, Naive Bayes) remain competitive on structured audio features, while deep models (CNNs, LSTMs, transformer hybrids) show improved representation learning for spectro-temporal inputs. Existing datasets and evaluations often suffer from small or imbalanced corpora, speaker overlap between train/test splits, limited accent diversity, lack of rigorous speaker-independent validation, and sparse robustness testing under realistic noise. Limitations include over-reliance on textual signals, insufficient feature engineering for prosody and accent, heavy data augmentation without careful hold-out evaluation, and insufficient comparison between classical and deep models under balanced, speaker- independent conditions. Abstract: This research addresses automated detection of hate speech in accented Malayalam audio by combining perceptually motivated acoustic features, controlled data augmentation, class-balancing, and a 1D convolutional neural network. We propose a structured pipeline that extracts a 162-dimensional acoustic feature vector per utterance (ZCR, STFT/chroma, MFCCs, RMS, mel spectrogram features), applies augmentation to increase accent diversity, and trains a speaker-independent model with SMOTE-based oversampling and class-weighted loss. The primary contribution is an end-to-end, accent-aware evaluation protocol that enforces speaker separation during cross-validation and measures robustness under Gaussian noise perturbation. Expected outcomes are improved detection performance and calibrated probabilistic discrimination over classical baselines (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) on an accented Malayalam corpus, a reproducible ablation analysis of feature groups and balancing strategies, and quantification of noise resilience. The framework is intended as a transferable methodology for hate-speech detection in low-resource, accent-rich speech domains. Experiments: Datasets: use the self-collected corpus described (original N=1,000; original class counts: 150 hate, 850 non-hate), augmented via noise injection/time-stretch/shift/pitch to produce augmented totals (hate ≈ 5,826; non-hate ≈ 2,322). Reserve an external unseen hold-out test set (15% of original speakers; maintain no speaker overlap) and a small external cross-dataset accented subset for cross-validation. Annotation: use existing consensus labels; retain speaker IDs for grouping. Preprocessing: z-score normalization; remove invalid entries; apply SMOTE only on training partitions. Models and baselines: 1D CNN (conv1d layers with filters [256,128,64], kernel size 5, max-pooling, dropout 0.2–0.3, dense 32/64, softmax; Adam lr=1e-3; early stopping), SVM with RBF kernel (grid search on C, gamma), Random Forest (100–200 trees, tune max_depth, min_samples_split), XGBoost and LightGBM (tuned learning rate, n_estimators, max_depth). Validation: perform speaker- independent 5-fold GroupKFold (group by speaker) and report hold-out results. Robustness test: add Gaussian noise (mu=0, sigma=0.05) to hold-out set. Evaluation metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (per class and macro), ROC AUC, confusion matrices, calibration curves; report mean and std across folds. Statistical testing: paired bootstrap or paired t-test on F1 between CNN and each baseline (alpha=0.05). Ablations: (A) feature-group ablation (MFCC-only, mel-spectrogram-only, chroma+ZCR-only, full 162-vector), (B) training ablation (with vs without SMOTE, with vs without class weights), (C) model ablation (CNN w/o dropout, CNN reduced filters), (D) augmentation ablation (no augmentation vs full augmentation). Hyperparameter tuning: grid/random search on validation folds; fixed random_seed for reproducibility. Reporting: provide per-fold metrics, aggregate means/std, confusion matrices, per-ablation delta in F1, and significance tests. Risk Factors and Limitations: Dataset bias: corpus sourced from films and YouTube may not represent spontaneous conversational speech or platform-specific language; class distribution after augmentation departs from natural prevalence. Annotation subjectivity: hate labels involve cultural/legal judgments and may contain residual disagreement despite high kappa. Synthetic oversampling (SMOTE) and aggressive augmentation can introduce distributional artifacts and risk overfitting to synthetic patterns. Speaker grouping limits: simulated speaker groups may not capture true population-level variability; small number of distinct speakers constrains generalization. Domain shift: models may fail on code-mixed, multilingual, or out-of-domain recordings. Noise and adversarial robustness: Gaussian noise tests do not cover real-world non-Gaussian background noise, reverberation, or adversarial perturbations. Evaluation bias: reporting high aggregated metrics can mask per-speaker or per-accent failure modes. Compute constraints: grid searches and ensemble models increase training time and resource needs, limiting replicability on low-resource hardware. Legal/ethical constraints: licensing (CC BY-NC-ND) and privacy considerations may restrict dataset sharing or derivative works. Finally, the approach is limited to audio-only signals and will not capture multimodal cues or contextual metadata that may be necessary for nuanced hate-speech judgments.
